c.tagline: Bangladesh's 'tea capital,' a rolling patchwork of tea gardens, pineapple groves, and rainforest reserves

card: Rarely accepted; cash is essential throughout

taxi.fareNote: CNG auto-rickshaws are the standard way to reach tea gardens and Lawachara National Park

emergency.note: 999 connects to police, fire, and ambulance across Bangladesh

religion: Christianity (small minority, notably among tea-garden communities)
walk: Central Sreemangal town is walkable; the tea gardens, Lawachara National Park, and outlying villages require a CNG auto-rickshaw or car

safety.safety: Very safe, welcoming rural area popular with domestic tourists
safety.crime: Very low crime; standard rural-travel common sense applies

hood_landmark.Sreemangal Town Center: Sreemangal's tea-stall row and central market
hood_landmark.Tea Garden Belt: The rolling Finlay and Deundi tea estates
hood_landmark.Lawachara National Park: Lawachara's rainforest canopy and hoolock gibbons

hood_desc: The small commercial hub with the famous seven-layer tea stalls, guesthouses, and the local market; the practical base for exploring the region.
Endless rolling hills of manicured tea bushes surrounding town, best explored by bicycle or rickshaw at sunrise or sunset.
A protected rainforest reserve a short drive from town, home to Bangladesh's rare hoolock gibbons and forest trekking trails.

water.note: Drink bottled or filtered water only.

transit.map: Not centrally published; hotels arrange transport to tea gardens and the national park
transit.note: Hiring a CNG for a half or full day is the standard way to see the tea gardens and Lawachara

transport.air: Sylhet Osmani International Airport (ZYL), about 1.5-2 hr away, is the nearest airport
transport.train: Direct train service from Dhaka and Sylhet to Sreemangal station
transport.bus: Frequent long-distance buses connect to Dhaka (about 4-5 hr) and Sylhet
transport.car: Reachable via the Dhaka-Sylhet highway; hiring a car with driver from Dhaka is common

net.m: Moderate 3G/4G in town, patchier in the tea gardens and forest
net.ap: A Grameenphone or Robi prepaid SIM

tip.s: Not customary but appreciated for guides, roughly 5-10%
tip.r: Not expected; rounding up is a nice gesture

food.name: Shatkora Beef Curry
food.desc: Sylhet's signature curry: beef slow-cooked with wedges of shatkora, a bitter-fragrant local citrus that cuts through the spice. Eaten with plain rice.

places.name: Kutum Bari Restaurant
places.note: Long-running town restaurant popular with travellers for Sylheti home cooking and shatkora curries.

places.name: Grand Sultan Tea Resort
places.note: The area's flagship resort kitchen, doing a refined version of regional dishes including shatkora beef.

places.name: Sreemangal town bazaar eateries
places.note: Cheap bhat-ghar canteens along the bazaar serving beef shatkora with rice at lunchtime.

food.name: Manipuri Kangshoi and Eromba
food.desc: Food of Srimangal's Manipuri community: kangshoi, a light vegetable-and-herb stew, and eromba, boiled vegetables mashed with fermented fish and chilli.

places.name: Manipuri Para kitchens
places.note: The Manipuri village beside Nilkantha; small home kitchens cook the community's own dishes.

places.name: Nishorgo Eco Resort
places.note: Eco-resort that arranges Manipuri and tribal meals for guests as part of village visits.

places.name: Kutum Bari Restaurant
places.note: Mixes Sylheti and tribal-influenced dishes; useful if you cannot get into a village kitchen.

food.name: Panch Phoron Vegetables and Dal
food.desc: Everyday tea-garden fare: seasonal vegetables and lentils tempered with panch phoron, the five-spice mix of fenugreek, nigella, cumin, fennel and mustard.

places.name: Sreemangal town bazaar eateries
places.note: Workers' canteens serving rice, dal and vegetable curries all day for a few taka.

places.name: Nishorgo Eco Resort
places.note: Home-style set meals of rice, dal and vegetables cooked for guests in the tea-garden setting.

places.name: Balishira Resort
places.note: Resort restaurant among the tea estates serving simple Bangladeshi thali-style meals.

food.name: Shutki Bhuna
food.desc: Sun-dried fish, often hidol or chepa, fried down hard with onion, garlic and green chilli into a pungent, intensely savoury Sylheti relish for rice.

places.name: Kutum Bari Restaurant
places.note: One of the more reliable places in town to order shutki cooked properly rather than timidly.

places.name: Sreemangal town bazaar eateries
places.note: Local bhat-ghars where shutki bhuna is a daily fixture; the dried fish is sold in the same bazaar.

places.name: Manipuri Para kitchens
places.note: Fermented and dried fish is central to Manipuri cooking here too, in a milder mashed form.

food.name: Srimangal Honey Pineapple
food.desc: The hill pineapples grown around Srimangal are famously sweet and low-acid, sold whole or cut with salt and chilli powder at roadside stalls in season.

places.name: Sreemangal town bazaar
places.note: Fruit sellers pile up local pineapple, jackfruit and lemon; peak season runs June to August.

places.name: Roadside stalls on the Kalighat tea-garden road
places.note: Stalls between the estates sell pineapple cut and spiced to order for passing visitors.

places.name: Lawachara road fruit stands
places.note: Stands on the way to the national park sell pineapple and lemon grown on the surrounding hills.

food.name: Bhorta Platter with Rice
food.desc: A spread of mashes, aloo, begun, dried fish, coriander and mustard oil, each mashed with chilli and served in small mounds around a plate of rice.

places.name: Kutum Bari Restaurant
places.note: Does a generous bhorta selection alongside curries; a good introduction to Sylheti flavours.

places.name: Sreemangal town bazaar eateries
places.note: Every rice canteen here builds a plate around four or five bhortas for very little money.

places.name: Balishira Resort
places.note: Serves bhorta platters to guests as part of set Bangladeshi meals.

food.name: Seven-Layer Tea
food.desc: Srimangal's own invention: seven distinct coloured, differently sweetened tea layers stacked in one glass without mixing. Created by Romesh Ram Gour.

places.name: Nilkantha Tea Cabin
places.note: The birthplace of seven-layer tea and still the definitive place to drink it; also does two- to six-layer glasses.

places.name: Nilkantha Tea Cabin (original branch)
places.note: The older, smaller cabin closer to town, quieter than the newer purpose-built one.

places.name: Roadside tea cabins on Station Road
places.note: Several imitators now serve layered tea in town; cheaper, and useful for comparison.

food.name: Tea-Garden Lebu Cha
food.desc: Strong black tea from the surrounding estates, taken plain, with milk, or as lebu cha with lemon, salt and green chilli. Srimangal grows most of it.

places.name: Nilkantha Tea Cabin
places.note: Also serves green, ginger, lemon and plain milk tea for a fraction of the layered price.

places.name: Estate tea stalls, Kalighat and Bhurbhuria gardens
places.note: Stalls at the garden gates pour the local leaf fresh; the cheapest and freshest cup in the district.

places.name: Grand Sultan Tea Resort
places.note: Serves single-estate teas from the surrounding gardens in a comfortable setting with tastings.

landmarks: Lawachara National Park
A lush semi-evergreen rainforest alive with endangered hoolock gibbons, where railway tracks cut cinematically through dense jungle just minutes from town.
Nilkantha Tea Cabin (seven-layer tea)
The legendary teahouse where Romesh Ram Gour invented seven-colour tea, serving rainbow-striped glasses that have become Srimangal's signature souvenir experience.
Madhabpur Lake
A serene lotus-and-lily-covered lake cradled by rolling tea gardens, offering some of the most photogenic hilltop viewpoints in Bangladesh's tea country.
Finlay Tea Estate
Endless emerald carpets of manicured tea bushes surround Srimangal, and this sprawling colonial-era estate is the classic place to watch pluckers at work.
Baikka Beel Wetland Sanctuary
A protected wetland on Hail Haor where observation towers overlook thousands of wintering waterbirds, lotus beds and glassy waters at sunrise.
Madhabkunda Waterfall
Bangladesh's most famous waterfall thunders 60 metres down a rocky amphitheatre in Moulvibazar, an easy and rewarding day trip from Srimangal.
Hum Hum Waterfall
A remote cascade hidden deep in the Rajkandi Reserve Forest, reached by an adventurous jungle trek through bamboo groves and streams.
Bangladesh Tea Research Institute
The scientific heart of the nation's tea industry, its experimental gardens and grounds open a window onto how the perfect cup is grown.
Khasia tribal villages (punjis)
Hilltop hamlets of the indigenous Khasia people, where betel-leaf vines climb forest trees and visitors glimpse a distinctive matrilineal way of life.
Hail Haor
A vast seasonal floodplain lake west of town where fishermen pole flat boats through reedbeds, spectacular during the monsoon and winter bird season.

train.note: Sreemangal Junction sits on the Dhaka-Akhaura-Sylhet main line and the train is the pleasantest way in: the Parabat, Joyantika and Kalni expresses take about 4-5 hours from Dhaka, the Upaban is the overnight option, and the Paharika and Udayan link Chattogram with Sylhet through the town. Book on eticket.railway.gov.bd as soon as the 10-day sales window opens, because the tea-country trains fill up at weekends and on holidays. Fares are low and the run through the hills is scenic, though delays of an hour or more are common. There are no international trains here - the cross-border services to India start in Dhaka and Khulna and have been suspended since July 2024.

bus.note: Coaches from Dhaka's Sayedabad and Fakirapool terminals - Shyamoli, Hanif, Ena and others - take about 4-5 hours to Srimangal, and frequent local buses cover the 1.5-hour hop from Sylhet. Tickets are sold at the operators' counters or online through Shohoz (https://www.shohoz.com/). No international coaches serve the town: services to Kolkata, Siliguri and Agartala leave from Dhaka, and the nearest land border is Tamabil-Dawki for Shillong, reached via Sylhet.

ferry.note: Srimangal is an inland tea-garden town in Moulvibazar district with no navigable waterway and no scheduled boats; the wetlands nearby, such as Hakaluki and Baikka Beel, are visited by hired country boats, which are excursions rather than transport.

half.name: Sylhet
half.blurb: Regional city known for the shrine of Hazrat Shah Jalal and surrounding tea estate hills.

full.name: Jaflong
full.blurb: Riverside stone-collecting area on the India border with the Khasi hills visible across the water.

full.name: Bichanakandi
full.blurb: Rocky riverbed spot near the Indian border with clear mountain streams and quarry boats.

full.name: Ratargul Swamp Forest
full.blurb: Freshwater swamp forest navigable by small boat between half-submerged trees during the wet season.
